He Bought This 1964 Mercury M-250 Pickup Truck for $900 After It Sat Parked for 40 Years
17 photos
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage
A car enthusiast, who has worked miracles on vehicles before, bought a 1964 Mercury M-250 pickup truck and is trying to return it to its former glory. The truck hasn't set wheels on the road for the past 40 years! In the meantime, its hood developed an entire ecosystem.
1987. That was when this 1964 Mercury M-250 pickup truck was last registered. It hasn't hit the road since. Brad Blakley of Grit & Iron Garage found it on Facebook Marketplace. He has never owned a Ford-built vehicle before, but there is always a first time for everything.
And it looks like he has started on the right foot, because Mercury trucks are quite an interesting chapter of Ford trucks’ history book. Ford produced a distinct lineup of Mercury-branded trucks from 1946 to 1968 specifically for the Canadian market. This allowed Canadian Lincoln-Mercury dealers to sell trucks alongside luxury cars.
By 1964, these trucks featured unique styling cues, like a distinct grille layout and Mercury lettering, while sharing the robust mechanics of Ford's legendary F-Series. The 1964 Mercury M-250 was sold exclusively in Canada. It was never offered by Ford Motor Company for sale to the general public in the United States.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage Back in mid-20th-century Canada, rural communities were massive, but populations were sparse. Ford Motor Company had two distinct dealership networks in Canada: Ford-Monarch and Lincoln-Mercury-Meteor.
Ford was worried about losing ground to General Motors, because many small towns only had one or the other. If a town only had a Lincoln-Mercury dealer, the residents of the area couldn’t buy a Ford F-Series truck. So Ford of Canada came up with the Mercury M-Series in 1946.
While the light-duty M-100 matched the light-duty Ford F-100, the M-250 was the heavy-duty 3/4-ton equivalent of the Ford F-250 . Ford sold hundreds of thousands of F-Series trucks in the U.S. and Canada, but Mercury M-Series trucks were sold strictly in Canada and only a fraction of those numbers. Finding a heavy-duty M-250 variant today is exceptionally rare.
Mechanically, the 1964 Mercury M-250 was built identically to the 1964 Ford F-250 as the firm made sure that parts were completely interchangeable. It was a robust, no-nonsense workhorse designed to handle brutal Canadian winters and rough farm terrain.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage The base engine was the 223-cubic-inch (3.7-liter) inline-six, the so-called "Mileage Maker," producing 135 horsepower (138 metric horsepower). The optional engine was the 352-cubic-inch (5.8-liter) FE Big-Block V8 with 220 horsepower (224 metric horsepower). A heavy-duty four-speed manual or a three-speed Cruise-O-Matic automatic put the power down.
The siblings rolled off the same production line, but came with distinct designs, starting with the grille. While the Ford trucks came with the massive "FORD" lettering across the front end, the 1964 Mercury grille featured the typical chrome format, and the front edge of the hood featured wide, individual chrome letters spelling out "MERCURY."
The Mercury truck was phased out in 1968, three years after the United States and Canada signed the Automotive Products Trade Agreement, which eliminated tariffs on vehicles built between the two countries, allowing Ford to cross-ship vehicles seamlessly across the border.
Because dealerships could now easily get whatever inventory they needed from either side of the border, the logistical need to manufacture a separate, low-volume Canadian truck line vanished. Production of the Mercury M-Series was officially halted in 1968.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage The truck that Brad ended up with is part of this story. The light-blue vehicle was originally listed for 1,000 Canadian dollars, but he negotiated it down to 900. He drove to the owner’s home with his new (well, not exactly new!) trailer to pick it up. He found it sitting behind some greenery, and by the way it looks, Mother Nature must have started to claim it.
Moss is growing on the hood, as if it’s indicating north with determination. Now, in Brad’s yard, it doesn't run, it doesn't drive, and it is sitting on flat tires, but the front bumper, which he mangled up when he unloaded the truck in his yard, was fixed up nicely after several failed attempts at pulling it back into its original shape with his tractor. He pulled, then hammered it down.
Brad tows it away with his tractor, with assistance from a stray cat that is probably looking for a home for her kittens soon to be born. Her favorite place turns out to be the bench seat inside the cabin. Can't blame her!
However, the cat did not help with anything but a scrutinizing look before Brad realized he used chains that were too short, and the truck did not have enough space to stop after he braked, and it stopped right in the tractor's bucket, which slightly damaged the hood that was already severely bitten by rust.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage Power washing alone wasn’t enough to clean the light-blue truck, given the thick moss blanketing the hood and the layer of mold covering almost everything else. Brad resorted to hand-scrubbing decades of grime and organic growth embedded into the body panels. It’s dirty work, but somebody's got to do it. His son Joey jumped in to lend a hand, proving to be far more helpful than the cat.
" I t looks like pretty cool-looking patina ," he concludes. However, it's not just rust that makes the hood look scarlet, but also moss that grew over the decades in which the truck sat untouched in someone's yard. However, removing everything that grew on the paint comes off with the paint.
The first wash (several washes, actually) in decades is just the beginning. Brad plans to make it run and drive, so it probably won't take long before it hits the road again for the first time in nearly 40 years.
